## Abstract

Brain injury is highly associated with preterm birth. Complications of prematurity, including spontaneous or necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC)-associated intestinal perforations, are linked to lifelong neurologic impairment yet the mechanisms are poorly understood. Early diagnosis of preterm brain injuries remains a significant challenge. Here, we identified subventricular zone echogenicity (SVE) on cranial ultrasound in preterm infants following intestinal perforations. The development of SVE was significantly associated with motor impairment at 2 years. SVE was replicated in a neonatal mouse model of intestinal perforation. Examination of the murine echogenic subventricular zone (SVZ) revealed NLRP3-inflammasome assembly in multiciliated FoxJ1+ ependymal cells and a loss of the ependymal border in this postnatal stem cell niche. These data suggest a mechanism of preterm brain injury localized to the SVZ that has not been adequately considered. Ultrasound detection of SVE may serve as an early biomarker for neurodevelopmental impairment after inflammatory disease in preterm infants.

## Abstract

Epstein and Janos et al. have identified subventricular zone echogenicity (SVE) in preterm infants with intestinal perforations. SVE was predictive of future motor impairment in affected infants. Using a mouse model, SVE was associated with an inflammatory injury to the ependymal layer that was associated with stem cell niche dysfunction.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Preterm birth is associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality and neurodevelopmental impairment (NDI) remains a significant long-term complication1–3. Common inflammatory intestinal diseases associated with prematurity, such as necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) or spontaneous intestinal perforation (SIP) have been linked to poor neurologic outcomes4–7. The etiology of NEC remains unclear but immature neonatal immunity, microbiome dysbiosis, and altered Toll-like 4 (TLR4) signaling appear to play important roles in the pathogenesis of this disease8. 50% of NEC cases will progress to intestinal perforation resulting in peritonitis, polymicrobial sepsis, or death9. About 5% of extremely low birthweight infants will develop SIP that occurs in the absence of NEC. While preterm infants who develop SIP lack most of the intestinal pathophysiology that characterizes perforated NEC (defined clinically as surgical NEC), they suffer similar adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes7. Surgical NEC and SIP similarly increase rates of cerebral palsy, cognitive impairment, psychomotor impairment, and neurosensory impairments in preterm survivors, suggesting that the perforations themselves contribute a unique risk and common pathophysiology resulting in abnormal brain development4,7,10.

There is mounting evidence that neuroinflammation is a contributing factor to brain injury following NEC11–14. Induction of nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasomes was reported in the brains of rodents following experimentally induced NEC, although the cellular source of these structures was not identified15. Inflammasomes are large multiprotein complexes assembled in response to infection- or stress- related signals and have been best studied in immune cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells16. Activated inflammasomes catalyze the cleavage of procaspase-1 which then cleaves both IL-1β and IL-18 to mature forms. NLRP3 inflammasomes also cleave members of the gasdermin (GSDM) protein family. Once cleaved, activated GSDMs assemble in the membrane forming pores resulting in a form of cell death called pyroptosis17,18.

The subventricular zone (SVZ) forms the periventricular border along the ventricular surface and forms the medial border of the germinal matrix located between the ventricles and the subcortical white matter dorsally and the caudate nucleus ventrally19. This structure serves multiple important roles in mammalian brain development20,21. The SVZ is of particular interest as this structure is tasked with the generation of glial restricted progenitor (GRP) populations that give rise to glia including astrocyte and oligodendrocyte lineages22–24. On the ventricular surface of the SVZ, multiciliated ependymal cells are organized into pinwheel structures forming the cellular barrier between the CSF and the neural stem/progenitor cells (NSPCs) niche25. In addition to forming a functional barrier between the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) and the stem cell compartment, ependymal cells directly regulate postnatal neurogenesis26. Beyond acting as a physical barrier between ventricular CSF and the stem cell niche, the multiciliated ependymal cells are responsible for maintaining CSF flow through the ventricular system and disruption of the CSF flow retards neuroblasts migration27,28. The B1 astrocyte population residing within the SVZ is the neural stem cell tasked with the generation of neuronal progenitors that are believed to migrate to the frontal lobes in infants via the medial migratory stream in postnatal early life29–31. The SVZ is also critical to the generation of glia through glial-restricted progenitors (GRPs)22,32. Postnatally, resident SVZ GRPs give rise to oligodendrocyte progenitors that are required for normal myelination in periventricular white matter regions33,34. Despite the critical function of SVZ in normal brain development, little research has focused on this region within the context of brain injury in preterm infants.

Non-hemorrhagic germinal matrix echogenicity has been noted on cranial ultrasounds (CUS) in preterm infants35,36 but has never been explained37. Here, we report an association between the development of subventricular zone echogenicity (SVE) and intestinal perforation in preterm infants and determine links to neurodevelopmental outcomes in patients with NEC or SIP. Using a neonatal mouse model of intestinal perforation (MIP), we replicated SVE and discovered an inflammatory injury to the SVZ niche. MIP induction leads to ependymal NLRP3 inflammasome assembly. Ependymal cell loss was associated with persistent disruptions in neurogenesis. We hypothesize that the sonographic finding of SVE in human infants may represent germinal matrix/SVZ inflammation or edema. The association of an observable injury to the postnatal SVZ and poor neurodevelopmental outcomes in preterm infants suggests a mechanism of brain injury that warrants further exploration as a possible biomarker or a previously unappreciated target for intervention.

## RESULTS

### Subventricular zone echogenicity (SVE) is associated with intestinal perforation.

We performed a retrospective review of all extremely low birth weight (ELBW) patients (≤ 1000 g) born at Duke University between 01/01/2017 and 12/31/2019 to test the association between clinical risk factors, including NEC, and subsequent development of the sonographic finding of SVE after adjusting for confounders. Of the 219 ELBW patients born during the period of study, 132 had a negative baseline CUS at the end of the first week of life excluding germinal matrix hemorrhage (GMH), and at least one additional follow up CUS, and were therefore included in the study. Three experienced pediatric radiologists reviewed all CUS studies and reported each as positive, negative or equivocal for SVE. There was strong agreement among the radiologists (Fleiss κ = 0.808 for positives and 0.696 overall) and so the combined SVE score was used for the remainder of the analysis.

The characteristics of the 132 patients are presented in table S1. Twenty-four/132 (18.2%) patients were positive for SVE with an average gestational age of 25.1 weeks (range 23.4–26.7). Representative CUS images for non-SVE and subsequent development of SVE in the same patient following NEC and intestinal perforation are shown (Figure 1A,B). Within our 3-year cohort, 12/24 (50%) of these positive cases had spontaneous or NEC-associated intestinal perforation prior to the appearance of SVE. Results of multinomial regression models to determine if SVE was significantly associated with the common complications of prematurity are presented in Figure 1C and table S2. Surgical NEC/bowel perforation was positively associated with positive combined SVE score compared to negative combined SVE score, after adjusting for gestational age, birthweight, and number of follow-up CUS (Figure 1C, adjusted OR: 4.81 (1.49, 15.6), p-value 0.009). No other complication analyzed was found to be significantly associated with the development of SVE (table S2). Additionally, sex was not found to be significantly different by combined SVE score (Fisher’s exact test p-value 0.959, table S1) and was not further examined in this analysis. Based on our retrospective analysis of the available CUS, the timing of SVE first detected after intestinal perforation ranged from 1–58 days after perforation. Three/12 (25%) of the positive patients had evidence of SVE on CUS within 10 days of perforation with 8/12 (66.7%) positive within 30 days of perforation.

In addition to the cohort of patients described above, we recently cared for an additional ELBW patient with no evidence of GMH on their initial CUS (Figure 1D). Following a complicated initial NICU course requiring multiple chest tubes for bilateral pneumothoraces, and gram-positive cocci bloodstream infection, the patient’s CUS remained negative for SVE on multiple imaging studies throughout this period. However, following the development of surgical NEC on day of life (DOL) 34, the patient developed subtle SVE within 2 weeks of the perforation that was pronounced by 1 month (Figure 1E,F). The SVE remained evident on subsequent CUS until past term equivalent age and multicystic evolution in the subventricular zone developed 3 months after the initial SVE observation (Figure 1G).

### SVE is associated with motor impairment in preterm infants with intestinal perforation.

To determine if SVE was associated with NDI in the intestinal perforation population, data were collected in infants ≤ 32 weeks gestational age born at DUHS and admitted to the NICU between 07/01/2000 and 12/31/2019 who had a history of surgical NEC or SIP. We identified 317 infants with this history, 174 of which were excluded because they had GMH on the initial CUS at the end of the first week, no CUS at the end of the first week to exclude GMH, or no follow-up CUS after the first week. Of the 143 remaining patients, 36 died in the first year, precluding formal clinical follow up. An additional 26 patients were excluded due to having risk factors of neurologic sequelae related to cystic PVL, postnatal stroke, or trisomy 21, leaving 81 patients to study for the association between SVE and NDI (Figure 1H). The characteristics of both the 143 intestinal perforation patients and the 81 NDI subset patients are presented in tables S3 & S4. Three experienced pediatric radiologists reviewed all CUS for all infants in this NEC cohort meeting inclusion criteria, and assigned both a categorical score (positive, negative, equivocal) and a 5-point Likert score (see Methods) to identify the patients’ SVE status. For the NEC cohort (N = 143) analysis the categorical scores (Fleiss κ = 0.832 for positives and 0.633 overall) were combined across radiologists and the Likert scores was averaged (ICC2 = 0.824). SVE was present in 49 of the 143 patients with intestinal perforation, and first detected at a mean of 18.7 days after perforation, with a range of −45 days to 107 days (Figure 1I). Three of the four patients in whom SVE was detected before intestinal perforation had a diagnosis of medical NEC before the positive CUS, possibly accounting for the finding.

The outcome of cognitive and motor NDI (normal, mild, significant) was measured via Bayley scales at 2 years. We hypothesized that development of SVE was associated with adverse neurodevelopment outcome in at-risk premature infants with a history of surgical NEC. To determine if SVE was associated with cognitive and motor NDI in patients with a history of intestinal perforation who survived to follow up, ordinal logistic regression models were fit to NDI and average SVE Likert after adjusting for gestational age. Since NDI was missing for 17/81 (21.0%) patients, complete case analyses were presented and compared to 2 multiple imputation methods which gave similar results (tables S5 & S6). In patients with a history of intestinal perforation, SVE was positively associated with motor impairment at 2 years, after adjusting for gestational age (Fig. 1J, aOR 1.55 (1.16, 2.08) p=0.003), but was not associated with cognitive NDI, after adjusting for gestational age (Figure 1J, aOR 1.29 (0.96, 1.74) p=0.095). Together, our data demonstrate a significant association of SVE with intestinal perforation in ELBW patients, and a significant association of SVE with motor NDI in premature infants with a history of intestinal perforation.

### Modeled Intestinal Perforation (MIP) replicates SVE in mice.

We have recently characterized a diffuse white matter injury in a neonatal mouse model of intestinal perforation (MIP) that shares many of the pathological features observed in preterm infants including motor deficits38. We utilize this clinically relevant model to determine if MIP induction in mice replicates the echogenicity observed in human preterm infants. Briefly, cecal contents (stool) from freshly sacrificed young stool donors were injected into the peritoneal cavity of recipient mice on postnatal day 5 (p5) to model neonatal spontaneous intestinal perforation. The p5 mouse brain development aligns with the developmental stage of a preterm 28-week gestational age infant39. We induced MIP in p5 mice and returned them to their dams to recover. Three days later (p9), we performed CUS on anesthetized mice to compare MIP mice to their control littermates (Figure 2A-D). CUS demonstrated significant increases in echogenicity (mean gray values) in the lateral wall of the lateral ventricles encompassing the postnatal SVZ in the MIP cohort (n=8) when compared to littermate controls (n=5, Figure. 2E,F, p<0.0001). These data suggest that changes in tissue characteristics resulting in SVE in humans following intestinal perforations (NEC or SIP) are mirrored in rodent MIP.

### Modeled Intestinal Perforation (MIP) induces NFκB-linked SVZ inflammation.

We next investigated the impact of neonatal MIP on peripheral inflammatory responses by measuring changes in NFκB-linked cytokine gene expression in the spleen using qPCR. Twenty-four hours following MIP induction, we observed systemic increases in Il1b, Tnf and Il6 transcripts (Figure 3A). NFκB-associated cytokine transcripts were elevated in multiple organ systems, including whole brain lysates38. We measured localized production of cytokine transcripts in the postnatal SVZ neural stem cell niche using qPCR to reveal elevations in Il1β and Tnfα localized to the SVZ at 24 hours following MIP induction (Figure 3B). We then performed single nuclei RNA sequencing (snRNA-Seq) on dissected SVZ tissue 48hrs after MIP induction and compared these data to age-matched control littermates. Transcriptomic analysis revealed 15 distinct cell clusters resident to the SVZ (Figure S1A-C). Stratifying the cells by experimental condition revealed an increase relative to total cell numbers in microglial (Tmem119+) and macrophage (Tmem119-CD68+Ly86+) lineages in MIP animals compared to control littermates (Figure S1D). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) from the macrophage cluster revealed an activated phenotype in SVZ-infiltrating macrophages with increases in complement and Fc receptor pathways (Figure 3C). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) performed on these cells confirmed a positive enrichment in multiple proinflammatory pathways, including IL-6 signaling, from MIP mice compared to controls (Figure 3D). IBA-1 immunostaining in coronal sections at 24 hours post-MIP induction revealed increases in microglia and macrophage infiltration of the SVZ and choroid plexus (Figure 3E). As an alternative approach to determine the organization of CD11b+ cells within the SVZ following MIP, we utilized transgenic FoxJ1-EGFP mice to express EGFP in the multiciliated ependymal cells residing on the ventricular surface of the SVZ. We induced MIP on p5 as above but stained whole mounted SVZ preparations to image the ventricular surface for EGFP (ependymal cells) and CD11b (macrophage/microglia).

Using confocal microscopy, we scanned the tissue from the ependymal surface through the first 50μm of tissue depth (Supplemental videos S1 and S2). In MIP mice, ameboid CD11b+ immune cells were observed on the ependymal surface and were abundant just below the surface of the ventricle. In contrast, control littermates showed no CD11b+ cells on the ventricular surface and only rare ramified CD11b+ cells below the surface in the SVZ. We next examined astrogliosis in the SVZ on p7, p10, and p25 following MIP induction (Figure S2 A-C). GFAP was significantly increased at p10 in the dorsal SVZ. The timing and dorsal distribution of astrogliosis aligns to the increased echogenicity seen on cranial ultrasound in mice following MIP. We subsequently immunostained our p25 control and MIP brains with antibodies against S100β, CD133, and GFAP to identify both ciliated ependymal cells and astrocytes along the ventricular surface. We identified regions of the ventricular wall that were devoid of ependymal cells and replaced with astrocytes that suggested the long-term outcome is a scarred SVZ (Figure S2D-G).

### Loss of SVZ ependymal cells following MIP

Using our whole mount approach combined with FoxJ1-EGFP alleles as above, we next analyzed changes to the ependymal surface of the SVZ 48hrs after MIP. Using antibodies against acetyl tubulin to identify ependymal cell cilia, we observed a loss of organized cilia on EGFP+ ependymal cells 48 hours after MIP induction compared to controls (Figure 3G). The expected pinwheel organization of EGFP+ ependymal cells were visualized throughout the ventricular surface in age-matched control mice at this time. In addition to the loss of cilia, MIP resulted in an ependymal cell layer that appears largely disorganized with areas devoid of cilia and ependymal cells when compared to controls (Figure 3G). We next performed scanning electron microscopy (SEM) on the ventricular surface of SVZ whole mounts in wild-type control animals and MIP littermates at 48hrs following MIP induction. As expected, the healthy ventricular surface is uniformly covered with cilia in p7 control animals (Figure 3H). SEM analysis of MIP littermates revealed large areas of the ventricular surface that were devoid of cilia similar to our findings using confocal microscopy (Figure 3H). Forkhead Box J1 (FoxJ1) is a well characterized transcription factor that is central to the generation and maintenance of multicilia in ependymal cells lining the SVZ40. Dissected SVZ tissue was subjected to western blot analysis to determine relative FoxJ1 protein levels between control and MIP littermates 24 hours after MIP induction (Figure 3I). When FoxJ1 is normalized to actin, we observed a significant (p = 0.039) decrease in FoxJ1 protein levels in the SVZ of mice with MIP (n = 11) compared to controls (n = 7, Figure 3J). Together, these data support our conclusion that there is a direct injury to the ependymal layer in the postnatal SVZ niche following modeled intestinal perforation in neonatal mice.

The SVZ niche is located adjacent to systemic structures such as choroid plexus and constitutes a potential immunologic gateway to the brain parenchyma41–43. We employed spatial in situ sequencing analysis (Xenium, 10X Genomics) of coronal brain tissue sections at 48 hours following MIP induction compared to control littermate to capture an unbiased perspective on transcriptomic changes adjacent to the SVZ niche (Figure 4A-C). MIP led to a loss of ependymal cells across the ventricular layer, compared to control (Figure 4C). CD68+ macrophages were visualized in the choroid plexus and on the surface of the SVZ following MIP compared to control sections (Figure 4C). Reactome GSEA analysis revealed multiple inflammatory pathways enriched in macrophages associated with the choroid plexus and in the SVZ (Figure 4D). Similar to our snRNAseq data, the GSEA of ependymal cell population from this spatial transcriptomics approach showed multiple TLR pathway enrichments (Figure 4E).

To assess the long-term loss of ependymal cells, we employed the FoxJ1-CreER allele crossed to a Rosa-26r TdTomato reporter line. In this model system, once the Rosa26r-TdTomato allele undergoes recombination at p3 (timing of tamoxifen injection), the expression of this reporter in the ependyma is divorced from the control of the FoxJ1 promoter allowing quantification of relative cell numbers independent of FoxJ1 promoter activity. We injected FoxJ1;TdTomato+ pups with tamoxifen on p3 and then randomized littermates into control and MIP groups on p5 (Figure 5A). Coronal sections of p25 brains revealed that by this timepoint, acetylated tubulin+ cilia are present on surviving ependymal cells (Figure 5B). Analysis of the ependymal surface in whole mounted control SVZ tissue at p35 revealed a high recombination rate of TdTomato in ependymal cells (Figure 5C). β-catenin immunostaining revealed a robust lateral border in these cells as expected. Analysis of the MIP cohort demonstrated a loss of TdTomato+ ependymal cells accompanied by a loss of organized β-catenin staining on the surface of the SVZ (Figure 5C). To quantify these findings over the entire SVZ, we generated single cell suspensions made from the SVZ in control and MIP animals at p27. Using a live-dead stain to gate on live cells, we measured the percentage of TdTomato+ ependymal cells relative to the entire population (Figure 5D). Percentages of TdTomato+ ependymal cells were normalized to control mice (n=4) and then compared to MIP mice (n=6). This analysis revealed about a 50% reduction in TdTomato+ ependymal cells in MIP mice compared to their control littermates that persists to at least 1 month following injury (Figure 5E).

### Ependymal cell NFκB activation and inflammasome assembly.

Using our SVZ snRNAseq data, we performed GSEA on the ependymal cell population and identified a depletion of the oxidative phosphorylation pathway and enrichment of the NFκB pathway (Figure 6A). We next investigated the functional impact of NFκB activation in primary ependymal cell cultures using LPS. Radial glia were harvested from wild type p0 pups and differentiated into ependymal cells in vitro as described26. To model inflammatory changes, we stimulated differentiated ependymal cells with 250ng/ml of ultra-pure LPS. At 2hrs and 6hrs following stimulation, we observed nuclear translocation of p65 to the nucleus in multiciliated ciliated cells suggesting activation of canonical NFκB signaling occurs in these ependymal cells (Figure 6B). qPCR analysis of NFκB-linked downstream pro-inflammatory genes Il-1β and Tnfα, revealed an increase in cytokine gene expression relative to control ependymal cells (Figure 6C,D). Immunostaining these primary ependymal cell cultures at 48 hours following LPS-stimulation demonstrated a disruption of β-catenin border staining similar to our in vivo findings and a marked loss of nuclear FoxJ1 protein (Figure 6E). Subsequent analysis confirmed a decrease of FoxJ1 protein at 2 and 6 days by western blot analysis and FoxJ1 mRNA levels (Figure 6F-H). The ciliary control genes, Ccdc and Ift, which are downstream of FoxJ1 were also significantly down regulated in ependymal cell cultures following LPS stimulation (Figure 6I,J). Cilia analysis using acetyl-tubulin immunostaining of ependymal cell cultures confirmed a loss of cilia in day 6 cultures treated with LPS (Figure 6K). These in vitro data replicate our in vivo ependymal cell findings and demonstrate that inflammatory environments result in ependymal NFκB signaling and a loss of gene expression linked to ciliary maintenance.

### Ependymal cell inflammasome assembly precedes cell death by pyroptosis

Because NFκB signaling was enriched in ependymal cells exposed to MIP in vivo or LPS in vitro we investigated the ability of this epithelial cell population to assemble and activate NFκB-linked inflammasomes. NLRP3 is a protein subunit of the inflammasome. We first analyzed SVZ tissue for Nlrp3 gene expression 24 hours after MIP induction. MIP animals demonstrated a significant increase in Nlrp3 transcripts relative to control littermates (Figure 7A). We next utilized an ASC-citrine allele to visualize inflammasome assembly in vivo following MIP induction44. The ASC-citrine allele fuses ASC, a protein component of inflammasomes, with the modified green fluorescent protein, citrine to localize the formation of inflammasomes to specific cell types. Tg-ASC-citrine pups were divided into control and MIP groups. Twenty-four hours after MIP induction, mice from control (n=3) and MIP groups (n=4) were used to generate whole mounts of the SVZ (Figure S3A). Immunostaining with the ependymal border protein, β-catenin allowed us to identify ependymal cells on the SVZ surface. While there were rare specks (2–3/SVZ wholemount) in the deep subependymal layer, no inflammasomes were visualized in the control animals at the ependymal level (Figure S3B,C). However, all MIP animals demonstrated multiple citrine+ ASC specks within the ependymal layer on the ventricular surface (Figure S3D,E). Specks were not uniformly produced across the ventricular surface but rather were localized to distinct regions that varied between mice. Speck counting in the ependymal cell layer revealed increased numbers of specks at 24 hours (average 27 specks/mm2) compared to 48 hours (14 specks/mm2) suggesting that this change occurs quickly after MIP induction (Figure S3F,G). To further evaluate inflammasome function in ependymal cells, we utilized our primary ependymal cell culture generated from p0 radial glia. Differentiated ependymal cells increased the inflammasome NLRP3 protein following LPS stimulation (Figure 7B,C). To determine if NLRP3 protein expression resulted in activated inflammasomes, we treated these ependymal cells with LPS followed by exposure to the NLRP3-inflammasome activator, nigericin. Activation was assessed by measuring cleavage of inflammasome targets IL-1β and Gasdermin D (GSDMD). Treatment of LPS-stimulated ependymal cells with nigericin resulted in cleavage of pro-IL-1β to its activated form p17 (Figure 7D,E). Notably, IL-1β cleavage was inhibited with the Caspase-1 inhibitor, YVAD-FMK (Figure 7F,G). In addition to IL-1β cleavage we observed cleavage of GSDMD following treatment with nigericin (Figure 7H,I). Cleaved GSDMD is a critical step to GSDMD pore formation leading to pyroptosis. To determine if ependymal cells undergo pyroptosis following inflammasome activation, we measured lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release into the media 45 minutes following nigericin stimulation. Ependymal cells release LDH into the media following nigericin treatment suggesting that these cells undergo pyroptosis following inflammasome activation (Figure 7J). Generating ependymal cell cultures from Tg-ASC-citrine mice, we were able identify activated inflammasomes in multiciliated ependymal cells in vitro (Figure 7K). When cells were stained with β-catenin to identify cell borders and acetylated tubulin to identify ciliated ependymal cells, inflammasome assembly was clearly observed in ependymal cells.

### MIP disrupts neuroblast chain organization

Previous reports suggest that a disruption of the ependymal cell layer in the SVZ was linked to abnormal neurogenesis and migration of neuroblasts26,27,45. To determine if the MIP-induced ependymal cell injury resulted in an expected disruption of neurogenesis, we analyzed our neuroblast and transient amplifying cells in our snRNAseq data. Our analysis revealed a decrease in both SVZ cell populations at 48 hours after MIP induction (Figure S1D). Plotting DEGs in a volcano plot reveals decreased expression in Tubb3 and Tuba1a which are critical genes involved in neuroblast migration (Figure S4A). In addition, EGFR is known to negatively regulate neuroblast migration46 and its expression is increased in MIP neuroblasts compared to controls. GSEA revealed enrichment in melanoma and ERBB signaling pathways which are both linked through EGFR signaling pathways in neuroblasts from MIP animals (Figure S4B). To further understand the impact of MIP on SVZ-derived neuroblasts, we induced MIP in wild-type mice at p5 and harvested the total RNA from SVZ tissues 11 days later at p16. qPCR for Dcx was similar between groups at this time point (Figure S4C). However, visual comparison of SVZ whole mount preparations immunostained for Dcx+ neuroblasts at p16 and again at p22 (n = 4/group) revealed abnormal neuroblast chain migration in MIP mice compared to their control littermates. We observed the characteristic neuroblast chains migrating up the lateral wall of the SVZ in all control animals studied (Figure S4D). Following MIP, we observed a loss of neuroblast chains at both p16 and p22 timepoints suggesting that MIP has a prolonged negative impact on neuroblast migration. These data strengthen our observation of ependymal cell injury and suggest that the level of damage is adequate to disrupt SVZ functions, such as neurogenesis.

### MIP induces motor impairment in mice

Our human data revealed an association between intestinal perforation and SVE in ELBW patients and an association between SVE and motor impairment in an intestinal perforation cohort. We next compared motor function in mice following neonatal MIP to their littermate controls using the CatWalk Gait Analysis System and tested for sex-associated differences. We generated control and MIP mice at p5 as above and performed gait analysis at 2 months of age (Figure S5A). Changes in overall speed at which the mice transverse the CatWalk or variations in that speed was not different between groups (Figure S5B). MIP mice demonstrated a significant reduction in their regularity index at adulthood. While both sexes demonstrated deficits in their regularity index, male mice were more affected when compared to their female counterparts (Figure S5C,D). Regularity index is a measure of interlimb coordination and motor planning. We identified mild MIP-associated gait disturbances including swing, swing speed, step cycle however, this was only observed in male mice (Figure S5E-J). The above data reveal that induction of MIP during the neonatal period results in motor deficits that persist into adulthood.

## DISCUSSION

Intestinal perforations are a common complication associated with preterm birth. Regardless of underlying etiology (NEC vs. SIP), 50% of survivors develop lifelong moderate to severe NDI47. Mechanisms linking systemic inflammation and preterm brain injury are largely unknown and timely diagnosis remains a challenge in neonatal medicine. Using our neonatal MIP model, we identified an echogenic inflammatory injury to the subventricular zone neural stem cell niche. We then performed a retrospective analysis of preterm infants and discovered that subventricular zone echogenicity (SVE) was associated with intestinal perforations and predicted future motor impairment. SVE may be the earliest imaging change observed in infants with intestinal perforations that may prognosticate neurologic outcomes. Our data suggest that SVZ injury may be an unrecognized pathogenic mechanism linking systemic inflammation to NDI in preterm infants.

The SVZ stem cell niche produces oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) required for normal myelin development23,48 or response to injury49–52. We provide evidence in human infants and mice that inflammatory injury to the SVZ was associated with future NDI. It is feasible that injury to the SVZ is an unrecognized contributor to myelination failure in preterm infants because the damaged SVZ fails to produce adequate numbers of OPCs in response to direct injury to these cells in white matter regions38. Inflammatory complications, such as NEC or SIP, that occur prior to 32 weeks gestational age are highly associated with hypomyelination throughout the subcortical and periventricular white matter. Diffuse white matter injury (DWMI) is the most common brain injury that is observed in survivors of medical NEC, surgical NEC, and SIP10,53–55. In addition to neuroinflammation, cardiovascular changes and associated brain perfusion deficits, independently or combined, have been implicated in preterm brain injuries. WMI in preterm infants take can several neuropathological forms ranging from cystic infarction known as cystic periventricular leukomalacia (PVL), or more focal areas of necrosis seen on neuroimaging as punctate white matter lesions (PWMLs) or a more diffuse form of white matter atrophy known as diffuse white matter injury (DWMI)56. While cystic PVL can be readily diagnosed with cranial ultrasound (CUS), its incidence is decreasing and now accounts for less than 5% of the total WMI burden observed in preterm infants57. MRI can identify PWML and DWMI, but the findings are subjective and limited to experienced academic medical centers. Although these MR findings can predict motor impairment, this prognostic information is only obtainable as infants approach term-equivalent age leaving a clear unmet need for early prognostic testing58–61.

MIP replicates many of the inflammatory changes and DWMI observed in infants with intestinal perforation including SVE. MIP induction results in a polymicrobial infection38,62,63 that initiates a robust systemic inflammatory response. Within 24 hours, we observed IBA-1+ monocytes/macrophages accumulating in the choroid plexus, a vascularized structure residing adjacent to the lateral ventricles. Here, the choroid plexus deposits activated macrophages directly onto the multiciliated surface of the SVZ resulting in an ependyma enriched for NFκB signaling. Ependymal NFκB activation leads to ubiquitination of FoxJ1, the central controller of multicilia64, leading to its degradation in proteosomes and subsequent loss of cilia45. NFκB-linked inflammasome component, NLRP365, is upregulated in vivo following MIP induction. We were able to identify assembled inflammasomes in the ependyma at 24 and 48 hours after MIP induction. Using primary ependymal cultures, we replicated many of the ependymal changes in vitro using LPS stimulation. Primary ependymal cells activate the NFκB pathway leading to ciliary degeneration. These cells assemble inflammasomes which become activated leading to the maturation of IL-1β and cleavage of GSDMD. Cleavage of GSDMD forms membrane pores leading to LDH release and cell death by pyroptosis66. In MIP mice, we observed a permanent loss of ependymal cells followed by the generation of astroglial scars in their place on the ventricular surface. To demonstrate a functional impact of this ependymal cell injury on SVZ physiology, we revealed a persistent migration deficit in Dcx+ neuronal progenitors.

Innovative approaches to early biomarkers for preterm brain injuries that predict NDI are needed in the NICU. Notably, almost 80% of ELBW neonates acquire a spectrum of preterm brain injury that is associated with complications of prematurity1–3. Many infants that survive intestinal perforations will be discharged from the NICU with “normal” appearing neuroimaging studies but will later exhibit developmental delays including motor deficits in the first year of life. Therefore, identifying and validating a biomarker that can predict NDI within 10 days of intestinal perforation will significantly advance neonatal medicine. The sonographic finding of bilaterally increased non-hemorrhagic SVE developing in this clinical setting, and regressing through a transient microcystic phase, holds promise as a biomarker for NDI. The finding has previously been described and has been variably attributed to late GMH, hyperechoic caudate nuclei, and sequelae of infection or ischemia35,36,67. Our study demonstrates its association with injury to the SVZ and NDI following NEC or SIP. We believe SVE may represent SVZ inflammation. Alternatively, SVE may be a result of sub-ependymal edema resulting from the loss of the ependymal border and their associated tight junctions that separate the CSF from the stem cell niche. Direct exposure of the niche to the free water content of CSF may lead to cellular swelling leading to stiffer tissue and echogenicity. Inflammation or edema as a cause for the sonographic finding of SVE is favored over hemorrhage, because unlike GMH, SVE occurs only after the first postnatal week, is always bilateral and symmetric, never extends into the ventricle, and in those infants who had concurrent MRI exams, there is no magnetic susceptibility artifact to suggest hemosiderin deposition characteristic of hemorrhage. MRI appears to offer no advantage to CUS in the detection of SVE; the spatial resolution of high frequency CUS is superior to that of brain MRI, and for the finding of SVE, CUS also provides superior contrast resolution.

Our demonstration of an association of SVE with NDI in this clinical setting supports a pathogenic mechanism linking NEC and brain injury in premature infants through injury to the postnatal SVZ stem cell niche. Two previous studies have looked for an association of SVE with NDI with conflicting results; both were small series which included cases of unilateral subventricular echogenicity67,68. One study of nine infants with SVE found lower psychomotor developmental scores than age-matched infants without SVE or GMH. Another study found no association between NDI and the subependymal cysts we found to be a transient characteristic phase of SVE before resolution.

While we are optimistic about the potential of SVE for both its mechanistic and prognostic implications, there are important limitations to our study. We suspect that this retrospective study underestimates the prevalence of SVE both because the finding was not yet understood or sought at the time of CUS in our retrospective cohorts, and because the CUS studies were obtained sporadically in our NEC cohort. The sporadic timing of the CUS studies also hampers detailed characterization of the timing and evolution of SVE, including the microcystic changes we found to be characteristic before resolution. While we determined that there was no sex effect in the development of SVE, we were unable to determine if sex was a determinant for NDI in infants due to incomplete data from our cohort. This question becomes more critical following our observation that male mice have worse motor outcomes compared to their female counterparts. While we hypothesize that SVZ injury is an unrecognized contributor to hypomyelination in preterm infants, future investigations will be needed to determine a direct association. These limitations highlight the need for prospective studies to better characterize this finding and to understand the precise implications of this injury on NDI in infants.

#### Primary cell cultures

Primary radial glia (ependymal cell) cultures were made from CD1 or ASC-citrine lines bred in house as previously described1. In brief, SVZ cells were dissected from postnatal day 1 up to postnatal day 3 animals of indicated strains, with dissected tissue finely diced, then gently triturated by using decreasing diameter sterile pipettes (1000 μl to 200 μl) to a single cell suspension. Cells from mouse SVZ were then diluted into 10 ml proliferation media using DMEM containing 10% FBS (HyClone) incubated in poly-D-lysine-coated plastic tissue-culture dishes or glass coverslips. Cells are grown at 37°C in 5% CO2 to near confluency with half-volume media changes daily. At ~95% confluency (3–5 days), media was removed and differentiated in DMEM containing 2% FBS for 7–10 days. Cells were then treated according to experimental conditions. Cells were fixed for either immunofluorescence with (4% PFA), lysed for polymerase chain reaction (RLT buffer) or western blotting (RIPA buffer).

### Method Details

#### Cranial ultrasound study of ELBW cohort.

A retrospective review was performed of all extremely low birth weight (ELBW) infants (≤ 1000 grams) born at our institution and admitted to the NICU between 1/1/2017 and 12/31/2019 (n=219). At our center, CUS are usually obtained at postnatal days 7 and 30 to screen for GMH and PVL, respectively. Those with germinal matrix hemorrhage on the initial CUS were excluded from the study, as were patients with structural anatomic abnormalities, and those who received no follow-up CUS. The CUS are performed by skilled pediatric sonographers on a Philips system with high frequency 8 MHz transducers. Standard coronal and sagittal plane images were obtained from the anterior fontanel.

CUS were retrospectively reviewed by 3 pediatric radiologists with 1, 4 and 29 years of experience. Each individual radiologist characterized each study as positive, equivocal or negative for SVE. A study was reported as positive for SVE if characteristic findings were seen in both coronal and sagittal planes. The findings in the coronal plane include symmetrically increased echogenicity medioventral to the caudate nuclei at the caudothalamic groove, extending anterior to choroid plexus in the roof of the midline third ventricle. In the sagittal plane, SVE is manifest as a rounded or tear-dropped echogenicity that extends anterior to the caudothalamic groove (Figure 1B). SVE characteristically evolved into multiple small microcysts (Figure 1G) before resolving completely. If the findings were equivocal, unilateral or seen in just one plane, or the characteristic microcystic change was seen on a late CUS without the earlier demonstration of SVE, the study was reported as equivocal. The 3 radiologist determinations for each patient were combined as follows: If 2/3 or 3/3 of readers reported a study as positive, the patient is rated as positive for combined SVE status. If 3/3 readers reported a study as negative, or 2 readers reported negative and one equivocal, the patient was rated as negative for combined SVE status. For all remaining combinations (EEE, EEN, EEP, NEP, NNP), the patient was rated as equivocal for combined SVE status. The three radiologists were blinded to the readings of the other two radiologists and to the exam’s initial interpretation. To assess interrater agreement among the 3 radiologists’ ratings for SVE in the N=132 patients, Fleiss’ Kappa was calculated.

For each patient included in the study, the following demographic data were retrieved from the medical record from the initial NICU admission: sex, race, gestational age, birth weight, small for gestational age (SGA) status, number of follow-up CUS, mortality, and postnatal age at time of death (table S1). Clinical risk factors were also retrieved for each patient: presence of spontaneous intestinal perforation (SIP)/surgical NEC, any positive blood culture, positive gram negative rod (GNR) blood culture or GNR UTI requiring treatment during NICU admission, clinical sepsis or infection requiring > 5 days of antibiotic therapy, retinopathy of prematurity requiring treatment with Avastin or laser therapy, chronic lung disease (CLD) of prematurity, surgical patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) ligation, APGAR scores at one and five minutes, cord blood gas at delivery, the presence of maternal infection/chorioamnionitis at the time of delivery, intrauterine growth restriction/fetal growth restriction (IUGR) status, and maternal preeclampsia. To test for the association between clinical risk factors and combined SVE score, multinomial logistic regression models (SAS 9.4) were fit to the risk factors adjusting for gestational age, birthweight, and the number of follow up CUS. For risk factors with missing values, models were fit on complete cases.

#### Cranial ultrasound study of intestinal perforation cohort.

A retrospective review was subsequently performed of premature (< 32.6 weeks) infants with diagnosis of surgical NEC/SIP at Duke University between 7/1/2000 and 12/31/2019 (n=317). Data acquisition was similar as above. Patients were included who had CUS at end of first week of life showing no GMH and at least one CUS after intestinal perforation. CUS were retrospectively reviewed by 3 pediatric radiologists with 2, 25 and 29 years of experience. Each radiologist rated each study for SVE with a 5-point Likert score (5 – symmetric subventricular echogenicity in both planes, new from prior, 4 – inability to confirm findings in 2nd plane due to incomplete documentation, 3 – equivocal findings, or definite findings in one plane, or on one side, 2 – equivocal findings in one plane, or one side, only, 1 – normal in both planes). The 3 radiologists’ determinations for the patients were combined by averaging their SVE Likert scores. The three radiologists were blinded to the readings of the other two radiologists and to the exam’s initial interpretation. To assess interrater agreement among the 3 radiologists’ ratings for SVE in the N=143, intraclass correlation was calculated for Likert scores and Fleiss’ Kappa was calculated for positive/equivocal/negative determinations. For each patient included in the study, the following demographic data were retrieved from the medical record: gestational age, birth weight, date of intestinal perforation and day of first appearance of SVE, sepsis, surgical intervention (drain or laparotomy), death in first year, and number of follow-up CUS (table S3).

#### Neurodevelopmental Impairment Assessment.

For the intestinal perforation cohort, the primary outcome was NDI at 18 to 22 months corrected age. NDI was defined as any of the following: moderate to severe cerebral palsy (CP) with Gross Motor Function Classification System level ≥2 or Bayley-III cognitive composite score <85. A comparison of the demographics between NDI subset and intestinal perforation cohort are compared in table S4. Seventeen/81 (21.0%) patients were missing data for cognitive and motor NDI due to leaving the clinic before assessment, doing well and not assessed, or for unknown reasons. To determine if SVE was associated with cognitive and motor NDI, ordinal logistic regression models adjusting for gestational age were fit to complete cases (R version 4.0.5). The proportional odds assumption was assessed using Brant’s test. Given the amount of missing data for cognitive and motor NDI (17/81, 21.0%), the complete case analysis was compared to 2 multiple imputation methods: 1) MI all, where all missing values were multiply imputed, and 2) MI left/unknown, where missing values for patients doing well were imputed as ‘normal’ and all other missing values were multiply imputed. Multiple imputation via fully conditional specification (mice package in R) was implemented including the following covariates in the imputation model: gestational age, corrected age at perf, birthweight, blood cultures, number of follow up CUS, average sve likert, cognitive, and motor NDI. M = 10 imputed datasets were created (via the ‘polyreg’ method) and the results were combined using Rubin’s rules, shown in tables S5 and S6.

#### Modeled Intestinal Perforation (MIP).

CD1 donor mice (age range p20-p25) were euthanized by CO2 to collect stool from the cecum. The cecal contents were weighed and resuspended in clinical grade 5% dextrose ½ normal saline to make a cecal slurry at a final concentration of 80 mg/mL. The cecal slurry was vortexed 3 times for 30 seconds and further disrupted using an 18G needle. The slurry was briefly centrifuged (10 seconds) on a mini tabletop centrifuge and used immediately (within 30 minutes). The recipient experimental pups were weighed and received a single intraperitoneal injection (i.p) of stool slurry using a 29G needle on postnatal day 5. The volume of the cecal slurry was 10μL/gram/mouse. Both male and female pups were used throughout our study.

#### In vivo mouse experiments.

Sepsis experiments were performed in C57Blk6J, ASC-citrine3 or FoxJ1-CreERT24 crossed with R26r-TdTomato with inhouse inbreeding. For the FoxJ1-CreERT2;R26r-TdTomato breeding, FoxJ1-CreERT2 heterozygote animals were bred to R26r-TdTomato homozygotes and verified with genotyping. For FoxJ1-CreERT2;R26r-TdTomato pups, tamoxifen was dissolved in MCT oil at 5mg/ml and administered subcutaneously between shoulder blades as a single 5mg/kg of body weight injected on P3. MIP is then induced as described above.

#### Cranial Ultrasound Studies in Mice.

Mice were bred at our facility. MIP was induced on p5 and pups were returned to their damn for 4 days. On p8–9, mice were anesthetized with and i.p. injection of 250mg/kg Avertin. Mice were imaged using a modified Vega robotic imaging system (SonoVol Inc., Durham, NC)5. The system consists of a dual-element wobbler transducer submerged in a hydrocarbon oil, with an optically and acoustically transparent membrane window on which the imaging target is placed (see Figure 2D). The wobbler transducer is mounted on a 2D motorized stage, allowing for automatic 3D imaging of samples. The wobbler transducer contains a low-frequency (~2 MHz) outer element and a high-frequency (~26 MHz) inner element that are concentrically aligned with a shared fixed-focal depth of 19 mm. In B-mode ultrasound, only the high-frequency inner element is used for both transmission and receiving of ultrasonic waves. The high-frequency element has a fractional bandwidth of ~87%, allowing for B-mode imaging in the range of 10–50 MHz. The pulse repetition frequency of the transducer is ~1 kHz with 256 A-lines acquired per frame, and a frame rate of ~13 Hz. Mice were placed on the transparent imaging window, with ultrasound gel used for acoustic coupling between the mouse head and the window. The position of the head was adjusted such that the focus of the transducer was approximately at the center of the brain. Individual scans were acquired at 10 MHz for this study to balance between the spatial resolution and imaging depth. For each elevational position, 20 B-mode images were averaged to increase the signal-to-noise ratio. The scan step size was 0.13 mm with a scan length of 15 mm and a lateral extent of 17.15 mm. The received ultrasound signals were post-processed with envelope extraction and log compression. The processed ultrasound images were used for further quantifying the echogenicity of the region of interest. The complete imaging sequence for each mouse took approximately 10 minutes.

#### SVZ wholemount.

Brain ventricular lateral wall wholemounts were isolated as previously described1,2. In brief, wild type or transgenic animals were euthanized by CO2 followed by decapitation according to IACUC protocols. Lateral ventricular surface was exposed by removing cerebellum, hippocampus, dorsal cortex, choroid plexus and midbrain, prior to fixing directly in paraformaldehyde solution (4%) for 24 hours. Tissue blocks were then permeabilized using 0.2% PBST solution and blocked with donkey serum at 10% in PBST and subsequent immunolabeling. Primary antibody solutions and fluorescently conjugated secondary were each incubated 48 hrs at 4 °C. SVZ whole mount was dissected from stained tissue hemisphere and mounted on Superfrost charged slides and cover-slipped with ProLong Glass Antifade mounting medium (Invitrogen).

#### Inflammasome activation.

ECs were generated as described above and stimulated with LPS-EB Ultrapure diluted in differentiation media to 250 ng/mL. Following 18 hours of LPS “priming” media was replaced with nigericin diluted to 5 uM in serum-free media. Experimental conditions including caspase-1 inhibition were incubated with YVAD-FMK (Selleck Chem) 60 minutes prior to and in conjunction with nigericin activation. Proteins were analyzed from mixed supernatants and cells collected in 4x Lamelli buffer after 45 minutes of nigericin stimulation for all experiments. LDH assay (Promega) were performed on supernatants and repeated in triplicates. To visualize inflammasome activation we used ASC-citrine mice3 to generate differentiated ependymal cells (EC) cultures from neonatal pups, as described above. ECs were cultured on poly-D-lysine coated coverslips and respective experimental condition were treated with LPS and nigericin as above. Coverslips and SVZ wholemounts were processed for immunofluorescence imaging using acetyl-tubulin and beta-catenin antibodies.

#### Quantitative PCR.

cDNA was prepared using High-Capacity cDNA RT (Applied Biosciences) from 0.5 or 1 microgram of total RNA. qPCR was performed using SYBR green (IQ SYBR green Supermix; Biorad) on a Biorad C1000 Touch Thermal Cycler using primers listed in Table S7. mRNA expression was calculated using the ΔΔCt method and normalized to β-actin or gapdh.

#### Western blotting.

Protein extract preparation and Western blotting were performed as described6. Chemiluminescence was visualized using the Syngene G:Box imaging system running GeneSys V1.4.1.0 (Syngene, MD). Blots were stripped using Restore Stripping Buffer (Biorad) and reprobed with anti-actin antibody. Bands of interest were quantified and normalized to actin in GeneTools Software (V4.03.04.0, Syngene, MD). Primary antibodies are listed in the Key Resources Table.

#### Immunostaining.

Preparation of brain tissue for whole mount immunohistochemistry (IHC) was as described above. For coronal sections: after transcardiac perfusion with 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1M phosphate buffer pH 7.4, brains were removed, post-fixed overnight, and cryoprotected in 30% sucrose at 4°C for 48hrs. Coronal 25 μm thick sections were serially cut on cryostat. For coverslips: at experimental endpoint media was replaced with 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1M phosphate buffer pH 7.4 for 25 minutes and then washed tree times in PBS. Samples were blocked for 1hr at room temperature (RT) in 0.2% PBST containing 10% normal donkey serum. Primary antibody incubation was carried out at 4°C in blocking buffer for 24hrs (coverslips and coronal sections) or 48hrs (whole mount), followed by incubation in appropriate Alexa Fluor secondary antibody (1:1,000) in blocking buffer for 2 hrs (coverslips or coronal sections) at RT or 24 hrs (whole mount) at 4°C. Nuclei was visualized with 4’,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (Dapi, Sigma). SVZ whole mount was dissected from stained tissue hemisphere and mounted on Superfrost charged slides with 3–4 drops of ProLong Glass Antifade mounting medium (Invitrogen) and covered with glass coverslip. Cell culture coverslips and coronal sections were mounted on Superfrost charged slides using ProLong Gold Antifade mounting medium (Invitrogen).

#### Confocal Imaging.

Images were obtained on a Leica SP8 confocal microscope. To generate large confocal composite images of the entire SVZ, we imaged on Leica SP8 confocal microscope using an oil emersion 40X objective. Images were collected using Leica Application Suite X (LAS X) navigator’s spiral function to give an overview. A region of interest that encompassed the entire lateral ventricular wall and SVZ was selected. Individual images were generated in 1024×1024 format with a 20% overlap between images. Images were then stitched together using LAS X with a smoothing function.

#### Electron microscopy.

Mice at P20 were perfused with 2% paraformaldehyde containing 0.1M sodium cacodylate, 2.5% glutaraldehyde, 2mM Ca2+ and 4mM Mg2+ at pH 7.4. Brains were postfixed in 2% glutaraldehyde containing 0.1M sodium cacodylate, 2mM Ca2+ and 4mM Mg2+ at pH 7.4 for 48 hours.

#### Single nuclei RNA sequencing.

The lateral walls of the lateral ventricles containing the SVZ were dissected and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80C until the analysis was performed. Drop-seq library preparation was carried out as per 10x Genomics’ recommendations for the 3’ Chromium Single Cell Gene Expression assay, version 1. Briefly, isolated SVZ nuclei from control littermates and septic mice were resuspended in a 1× PBS / 0.04% BSA solution, at a concentration of 1000 cells/µl. After size selection (<50 µm), the cell suspensions were washed with a 1× PBS / 0.04% BSA solution to remove debris, clumps, dead cells and contaminants, and a Countess II automated cell counter (Thermofisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) used to determine the cell concentration and the solution normalized to 1×106 cells/ml. Cell preps were titrated to contain ~3000 cells per library. Cells were combined with a master mix that contains reverse transcription reagents and loaded onto the 10X Chromium Controller instrument (10X Genomics, Inc., Pleasanton, CA) along with gel beads carrying the Illumina P7 and R2 primers, a 14-bp identifying barcode, a 10-bp randomer for RNA molecule quantitation, and a poly-dT primer and oil for the partitioning. Cells were inserted into nanoliter-scale oil emulsions with the gel beads (GEMS), within which reverse-transcription is carried out and all poly-a transcripts within a GEM, i.e. from one cell, share a common barcode. After the RT reaction, the GEMs were broken and the full-length cDNAs cleaned with Silane Dynabeads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) and then amplified. Amplified cDNA was purified with SPRI beads (Beckman Coulter Life Sciences, Indianapolis IN). After purification, the cDNAs were run on the Agilent Bioanalyzer High Sensitivity chip (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) for qualitative analysis. cDNA was sheared to ~200-bp with a Covaris S220 Focused-ultrasonicator (Covaris, Inc., Woburn, MA) and then sequencing libraries constructed for running on an Illumina high-throughput sequencer. This entailed end repair and A-tailing, P5 adapter ligation, SPRI bead clean-up, a sample index PCR, and further SPRI bead clean-ups. The sample index PCR adds a unique sample index for sample multiplexing during sequencing, with P5 and P7 primers used in Illumina bridge amplification. The sequence was generated using 125-bp paired-end sequencing on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 sequencing platform (Illumina, Inc., San Diego, CA) at the Duke Center for Genomics and Computational Biology sequencing core.

#### Single cell sequence cell data analysis.

Data from the two samples (control SVZ and septic SVZ) were initially processed using recommended protocols and software (Cell Ranger v5.0.1, 10x Genomics). These steps involved the creation and processing of FASTQ files through the demultiplexing of raw reads, aligning reads to the mouse transcriptome (mm10–2020-A) downloaded from 10X reference transcript repository, flagging PCR duplicate reads, and filtering out non-cellular reads. Cell Ranger then converted this processed data into a single filtered gene-barcode expression matrix that included data from each sample individually. We performed further downstream analyses using this expression matrix via the R package Seurat (http://satijalab.org/seurat/; v4.0.1). Minimum gene and barcode observance thresholds were applied in order to remove rarely-expressed genes and barcodes that expressed low numbers of genes, with additional filtering being applied at the barcode-level in order to remove barcodes that likely represented multiplets (i.e. barcodes that reflect situations where multiple cells were captured and sequenced within a single emulsified gel bead) from further analysis. After log normalization and scaling, the most variably expressed genes in our data were identified and utilized in integrating the samples. Using Seurat’s FindIntegrationAnchors() and IntegrateData() function, both samples were combined/integrated as one dataset for further analysis. Significant principal components (PCs) were calculated for scaled integrated data using RunPCA() function in Seurat and most significant PCs were selected based on visualization via Heatmap. Significant PCs were carried forward in analysis and used as input for unsupervised graph-based clustering (Seurat’s FindClusters function), which assigned each cell to a discrete cluster identity, and visualization of cells was achieved through the use of manifold learning technique UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection), which allowed the information captured by the significant PCs to be reduced and represented in 2 dimensions. The results of these analyses can be visualized in Fig. 2B. Further analyses involved examining the cellular distribution of expression of a priori genes of interest, as well as identifying and exploring genes determined to be associated with assigned cell cluster identities.

#### Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA).

From Molecular Signature Database (MSigDB), Hallmark and KEGG gene sets were used to check differential pathways regulation using gene list obtained for cell types of interest when compared between MIP and control samples. Fgsea packages was used in R to find enriched gene sets with default parameter and resulting pathways were filtered as significant with p.adj < 0.05.

#### Spatial Transcriptomics.

Coronal sections of 7 day old mouse brains that were formalin fixed and paraffin embedded (FFPE) were sectioned at 5um and placed on 10x Genomics Xenium slides for deparaffinization and decrosslinking. Processed slides were then loaded for imaging on a Xenium Analyzer (10xGenomics, Pleasanton, CA) for in situ sequencing analysis using a targeted gene panel of 296 genes. Cyclical rounds of fluorescent padlock probe hybridization, imaging, and removal generated optical patterns specific for each transcript barcodes, which were then converted into gene identities and visualized using Xenium Explorer software7. Image analysis involved pre-processing, puncta detection, transcript decoding and the assignment of quality scores. In silico cell segmentation was performed using DAPI-stained images of submitted sections to detect nuclei and expanded outwards until either 15 um max distance is reached, or the boundary of another cell is reached. Feature-cell matrix, transcript coordinates and cell boundaries were used for downstream analysis using Seurat8. Data was formatted in the Seurat object format for quality control and then normalized using SCTransform function. To identify clusters, neighborhood graphs were computed considering principal components and cell-type annotations using differentially expressed canonical gene list using FindAllMarker function from Seurat9. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were calculated between the sections using Seurat’s FindMarker function for each cell type and were plotted using Enhanced Volcano package in R. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was used to characterize differentially expressed pathways between experimental conditions10.

#### SVZ flow cytometry.

Flow cytometry was performed on single-cell suspensions from SVZ dissected from FoxJ1-CreERT2;R26r-TdTomato mice, as described above. Mice were euthanized on p27 and the brain lateral ventricular wall was dissected and processed into single cell suspension using the Neural Dissociation Kit (Miltenyi). Samples were incubated with Viobility live/dead marker (Miltenyi) prior to fixation. Flow cytometry of tdTomato+ cell populations was performed on MA900 Multi-Application Cell Sorter (Sony Biotechnology Inc.) at the Duke Flow Cytometry Research Core. Analysis was performed on FlowJo™ v10 Software (BD Life Sciences). The data were analyzed in a conventional method using forward scattered (FSC) and back scattered (BSC) laser light to first eliminate debris. Sequential gating was employed using the FSC-width and FSC-area signals to eliminate doublets followed by gating on live cells identified using Viobility Live/Dead marker (Miltenyi) in the 450/50 detector. Finally, cells were counted that expressed the compensated tdTomato signal in the 585/30 detector. Over 10,000 live cell events were collected per sample.

### Quantification and Statistical Analysis

#### Statistics.

Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m., unless otherwise indicated. Statistical analyses were performed using Prism software. Student’s t-test, Fisher’s exact test, or one way ANOVA with post hoc tests were performed as indicated. Significance was defined as P<0.05. Sample sizes were estimated empirically or based on power calculations. Blinding was used for all analyses comparing control mice and treated mice.
